metaDesc: Full guide to Pang Ung, the misty pine-forest reservoir in Mae Hong Son, Thailand. How to book the campsite, prices, homestays, getting there from town, and the best time to catch the morning fog.
keywords: Pang Ung, Pang Ung Mae Hong Son, Pang Ung camping, Pang Ung accommodation, Pang Ung morning mist, how to get to Pang Ung
h1:
Pang Ung
Morning Mist, Pine Forest & a Lake in the Valley
intro: Pang Ung is a small reservoir ringed by pine forest on a high ridge near the Myanmar border. Before dawn, mist drifts across the water like a sheet and the first light cuts through the pine tops — which is why people started calling it the Switzerland of Thailand. We've pulled together everything you need to know before you go: camping, where to stay, how to get there, and when the fog actually shows up.

blocks.html: Pang Ung sits in Ban Ruam Thai, Mok Cham Pae sub-district, about 44 kilometres from Mae Hong Son town — but it's a winding mountain road, so the real drive takes almost 2 hours. The area is managed under Tham Pla–Pha Suea Waterfall National Park. The spot everyone photographs is the reservoir with pines growing all around it, plus a lakeside campsite where you can stay overnight. The real magic here happens before dawn, when the fog is still thick and the air is bitterly cold.

Pang Ung isn't impressive because of its size — the reservoir is smaller than most people expect. What makes people willing to drive this far is the early-morning atmosphere: mist hovering over the still water with the pines mirrored below. You won't find that scene in many places in Thailand. In the cold season, there are white and black swans the park keeps on the water — a photo corner people fall for.

items: Morning mist at first light — the real highlight. You have to be up before dawn to catch it.
Three-needle pine forest — walk and shoot photos all the way around the lake; the air stays cool all day.
Bamboo raft rides — there's a service that paddles you around the reservoir in the morning, at a friendly price.
Right next to Ban Rak Thai — drive on about 6 more kilometres to reach the Yunnanese Chinese tea village; you can do both on one trip.

blocks.title: Best time to go
blocks.html: The mist is at its best from November to February, when it gets seriously cold — pre-dawn temperatures have dropped below 10°C. In the rainy season (June–Oct) the forest is lush and green, but the roads are slippery and the fog is hit or miss. If you're here for the mist photos, go in the cold season.

blocks.text: Camping at Pang Ung — how to book and what it costs

blocks.html: The Pang Ung campsite is run by the National Parks Department and opens for camping from 1 October each year, which lines up nicely with the start of the cold season. You have to book in advance through the department's online booking site (nps.dnp.go.th) — not on the spot — because high season gets very busy and the site fills up fast. We'd book several weeks ahead, especially for long weekends and New Year.

items: Bring your own tent — the site fee is around 30 THB per person per night.
Rent a park tent — rentals start around 225 THB per night (size and price vary by tent; check again on the booking page).
Facilities — separate men's and women's toilets with showers, staff on site, and a cooking area.
Food near the campsite — local vendors sell breakfast and coffee, so you don't have to haul in all your own supplies.

blocks.title: Before you sleep in a tent
blocks.html: Nights and early mornings are far colder than you'd expect — your sleeping bag genuinely needs to handle the cold, and pack a wool hat and gloves too. A torch or headlamp is essential, because there's almost no light in the middle of the night and the phone signal is patchy. Tell someone at home before you head up the mountain.

blocks.text: Where to stay at Pang Ung if you're not camping

blocks.html: If you'd rather not sleep in a tent, the area around Pang Ung and Ban Rak Thai has plenty of homestays and local guesthouses — from simple adobe houses to wooden cabins by the reservoir. Prices start from a few hundred up to the low thousands of THB per night. Most are local places you book through Facebook or by calling directly, though some are listed on online booking platforms.

items.name: Lakeside homestay at Pang Ung
items.blurb: A local guesthouse close to the reservoir — a few minutes' walk to the mist-viewing spot. Good if you want to be up early shooting photos without having to drive.

items.name: Stays around Ban Rak Thai
items.blurb: The Yunnanese Chinese tea village just past Pang Ung has lodging by a pond with tea-plantation views. Do Pang Ung in the morning and come back to sleep at Ban Rak Thai.

items.name: Adobe-house homestay
items.blurb: Cool adobe-style rooms, simple and surrounded by nature, at a friendly price. Good for backpackers and small families.

blocks.title: Always book ahead
blocks.html: There aren't many places to stay around Pang Ung, and they fill up fast in the cold season. If you're planning to go in December–January, book at least 2–4 weeks ahead and confirm clearly with the owner before you set off.

Pang Ung is up in the mountains, and the road up is a continuous string of curves, steep in places. Whether you drive yourself or take a local truck, leave extra time and brace yourself for the switchbacks. Here are the main options from Mae Hong Son town.

items: Self-drive / car rental — take the Mae Hong Son–Pai route (Highway 1095). About 15 km out of town there's a left turn signposted to Pho Khlon; turn in on the same road, then keep climbing up to Pang Ung and Ban Rak Thai. A sedan can make it, but drive carefully.
Motorbike — popular with road-trippers; the views are great the whole way, but it's steep with lots of curves. You need to be genuinely confident riding, and check your brakes first.

Yellow songthaew — these run from Sai Yud Market in town. Uphill departures at 9:00 and 15:30; downhill at 5:30 and 11:00. Good if you don't have a vehicle, but plan your timing carefully because the runs are limited.
Chartered vehicle — chartering a ride from town out to Ban Rak Thai–Pang Ung runs around 1,500 THB. Comfortable and flexible on timing — good for groups of friends or families.

blocks.title: What people usually get wrong
blocks.html: Don't drive up the mountain at night if you don't know the road — it's very dark and unlit. Aim to arrive before dusk, and fill up your tank before leaving town, because fuel stations up the mountain are few and close early.

Pang Ung is best when you stay overnight, because the highlight is the morning mist — go up and back in a day and you'll miss the best part. Here's a well-paced plan for 2 days and 1 night, including Ban Rak Thai right next door.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Up the mountain–Ban Rak Thai–check in

items.activity: Leave Mae Hong Son town and drive up Highway 1095, past the Pho Khlon junction and up the mountain.
items.note: Fill up the tank before you go

items.activity: Stop at Pho Khlon or a viewpoint along the way to stretch your legs before the long climb.
Reach Ban Rak Thai for stewed pork leg with mantou buns and Yunnanese tea by the pond.
items.note: Several pork-leg shops in the village — all of them are great

items.activity: Walk the tea plantation, taste some tea, photograph the village, then check in to your stay or the Pang Ung campsite.
Sunset over the reservoir, dinner, then an early night.
items.note: Tomorrow you have to be up before dawn

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Pang Ung morning mist–raft ride–drive down

items.activity: Get up to catch the morning mist over the reservoir and wait for the first light to cut through the pine tops.
items.note: Wear a heavy jacket — your hands will freeze without gloves

items.activity: Take a bamboo raft around the reservoir, photograph the swans, then grab coffee at a lakeside local stall.
Pack up and take a walk through the pine forest before checking out.
Drive back down the mountain to Mae Hong Son town, stopping for the viewpoint photos you missed yesterday.
items.note: Watch your brakes on the way down; use low gear on the steep sections

blocks.text: A few last things before you go

items: Bring enough cash — there are almost no ATMs up the mountain and some shops only take cash.
Phone signal is limited; download offline maps before heading up.
Pack your regular medications and something for motion sickness, since there are a lot of curves.
Take your rubbish back down with you to help keep the area clean.

faq.q: What time should I arrive at Pang Ung to see the mist?
faq.a: The mist is best before dawn, roughly 5:30 to 6:30 AM. Once the first light comes up the fog gradually fades, so staying overnight at Pang Ung or Ban Rak Thai is far better value than going up and back in a day. The fog is thickest in the cold season, November to February.

faq.q: Do I need to book Pang Ung camping in advance?
faq.a: Yes — book ahead through the National Parks Department site (nps.dnp.go.th). The campsite opens from 1 October each year. High season, especially long weekends and New Year, gets very crowded and fills fast, so book several weeks ahead. If you bring your own tent, the site fee is around 30 THB per person per night.

faq.q: I don't have my own vehicle — how do I get to Pang Ung?
faq.a: There are yellow songthaews from Sai Yud Market in Mae Hong Son town: uphill at 9:00 and 15:30, downhill at 5:30 and 11:00. Or you can charter a ride from town to Ban Rak Thai–Pang Ung for around 1,500 THB, which is much more flexible on timing.

faq.q: How cold does Pang Ung get, and what should I bring?
faq.a: In the cold season, pre-dawn temperatures have dropped below 10°C. If you're sleeping in a tent, your sleeping bag genuinely needs to handle the cold — pack a wool hat, gloves and a heavy jacket. A torch or headlamp is essential since there's almost no light at night, and bring enough cash because ATMs are hard to find up the mountain.

faq.q: Can I visit Pang Ung and Ban Rak Thai on the same trip?
faq.a: Yes, and we'd recommend pairing them, because Ban Rak Thai is only about 6 kilometres past Pang Ung. The popular plan is to visit Ban Rak Thai in the afternoon for stewed pork leg with mantou and Yunnanese tea, then stay the night near Pang Ung and get up early for the mist over the reservoir.
